issues.legal_issue: A person claiming tenancy rights solely as a legatee is not an heir who succeeds to a residential tenancy under the statutory succession provision.
material_facts: In both appeals, the claimant relied on a will purporting to bequeath the deceased tenant’s tenancy rights and did not claim to qualify as a family member who had resided with the tenant at death.
In the disputed premises, family members or other occupants had been residing with the deceased tenants at the time of their deaths.
The claimants brought eviction suits on the basis of the bequests, and the High Courts rejected those claims.
issues.conclusion: The word “heir” in the residential-tenancy succession provision does not include a legatee; a claimant cannot obtain tenant status under that provision solely by taking under a will.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 5(11)(c)(i) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a family member residing with the tenant at death has priority to be treated as tenant; only in the absence of such a member may an heir be selected, with the court deciding in default of agreement. The statutory scheme and the words providing for court selection concern heirs succeeding under ordinary succession, not testamentary legatees, whose inclusion could defeat the statutory priority and render the court-selection provision ineffective. The meaning of “heir” depends on the scheme and purpose of the legislation, as recognized in Jaspal Singh v. District Judge. The Court followed Bhavarlal L. Shah v. Kanaiyalal N. Intawala, which approved Anant T. Sabnis (Dr) v. Vasant Pratap Pandit. The Court also rejected the contention that this interpretation impermissibly discriminates between family members claiming under a will and those claiming by intestate succession.

predicates.residential_tenancy_succession_case: The dispute concerns who succeeds to a deceased tenant’s rights in premises let for residence.
predicates.claimant_relies_on_will: The claimant bases the claim to the deceased tenant’s tenancy rights on a testamentary gift.
predicates.claimant_qualifies_as_resident_family_me: The claimant is a member of the tenant’s family who resided with the tenant when the tenant died.

issues.definition: When a residential-tenancy succession dispute is based on a will and the claimant does not qualify as a resident family member, the claimant does not succeed as tenant merely as a legatee.

issues.legal_issue: A testamentary bequest of tenancy rights falls within the statutory restriction on assigning or transferring tenancy rights.
material_facts: The deceased tenants’ wills purported to bequeath their tenancy rights in the premises.
The claimants sought to rely on those bequests to assert rights in the tenancies.
The dispute concerned residential premises governed by rent-control legislation.
issues.conclusion: The statutory restriction on assignment or transfer includes a transfer by testamentary bequest, so the bequests could not confer the claimed tenancy rights.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 prohibits a tenant from assigning or transferring the premises, subject to a contract to the contrary. The phrase “in any other manner” gives “transfer” a generic meaning broad enough to include a testamentary transfer. The Transfer of Property Act’s treatment of transfers inter vivos does not govern the meaning of “transfer” under this rent-control legislation. The Court followed Bhavarlal L. Shah v. Kanaiyalal N. Intawala and the reasoning approved there from Anant T. Sabnis (Dr) v. Vasant Pratap Pandit.

predicates.rent_control_tenancy_dispute: The dispute concerns tenancy rights in premises governed by rent-control legislation.
predicates.tenant_bequeaths_tenancy_rights: A tenant purports by will to pass tenancy rights in the premises to another person.

issues.definition: When a tenant in a rent-control tenancy dispute purports to bequeath tenancy rights, the bequest falls within the restriction on transfers.
